passage: Joseph's diary, Tuesday. Reena held my hand while we walked to the bus, like she does with all her friends. Some boys said, “Boyfriend-girlfriend!” That's silly. It's just how we walk together. Sir also patted my back after the quiz and said, “Well done.” That felt nice too, like he was happy for me. But at the gate today I didn't feel like holding hands. I said, “Not today,” and Reena said, “Okay,” and swung her bag. It felt good that I could say that. Mum says if any touch feels off, I can say no and tell her.

qa.q: What did Sir do after the quiz?
qa.a: Sir patted Joseph's back and said, “Well done.”

qa.q: What did Joseph think Reena's hand-holding and Sir's pat meant, and how did he feel?
qa.a: Joseph took them as friendship and reassurance, and the pat felt like Sir was happy for Joseph. Joseph did not treat them as romance.

qa.q: What did Joseph do at the gate, and what does Joseph's mum say?
qa.a: Joseph said “Not today” when hand-holding didn't feel right, and Reena accepted it. Mum says Joseph can say no to any touch that feels off and tell her.

qa.q: How might Reena feel when Joseph says “Not today”?
qa.a: Probably fine with it, since she said “Okay” and swung her bag. She may simply have accepted that Joseph wanted a different day.

grounding: Hand-holding and pats among friends show friendship, and a child can refuse any touch that feels off.

passage:
In the village school, Gurpreet Sir gave Madhuri a light pat on the shoulder after her recitation. “Well done.” Madhuri smiled. She and her friend Sarita walked to the pump arm in arm, as always.
Later, a visitor who was leaving the school pinched Madhuri's cheek and laughed. Madhuri frowned and pulled back. Gurpreet Sir noticed. When the visitor had gone, he said, “Did you like that?”
“No,” said Madhuri.
“You can say no to any touch you don't like, and you can always tell me. I'll listen.”

qa.q: Where did Madhuri and Sarita walk arm in arm?
qa.a: They walked to the pump.

qa.q: What did Madhuri feel about the pat from Gurpreet Sir compared with the pinch on her cheek?
qa.a: She smiled at the pat, which seemed to reassure her. She frowned and pulled back from the pinch, so she did not like it.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet Sir do that protects Madhuri?
qa.a: He noticed her pulling back, asked if she liked it, and told her she can say no to any touch she doesn't like and tell him.

qa.q: How might the visitor have seen the cheek pinch?
qa.a: Possibly as a friendly gesture, without noticing that Madhuri did not like it. That is why saying no matters.

grounding: Pats and hand-holding among friends show warmth; unwanted touch can be refused and reported.

passage: In Kaito's first month at the school in São Paulo, his new friend Paulo walked him to the canteen every day with an arm slung round his shoulders. Kaito's whole body went stiff. Back in Osaka, boys didn't do that. Did Paulo think he was a baby? Then he watched the playground: boys walking arm in arm, girls holding hands, a teacher patting a crying child's back. Here, it was just friendship. Still, the arm felt like too much. On Friday he said, “Paulo, can we just walk side by side? I'm not used to it.” Paulo let go at once. “Sure! Sorry.” He grinned and bumped Kaito's elbow instead. Kaito laughed.

qa.q: Where did Paulo walk Kaito every day?
qa.a: Paulo walked him to the canteen every day.

qa.q: What was Kaito feeling when his body went stiff?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable and unsure, worried Paulo thought he was a baby, because such touch wasn't usual where he grew up.

qa.q: What did Kaito do that was wise?
qa.a: He watched how others touched to understand it meant friendship, then politely asked Paulo to walk side by side instead.

qa.q: How did Paulo respond, and what does that show?
qa.a: Paulo let go at once and apologised, showing he meant only friendship and respected Kaito's wish.

grounding: Shows a child reading a friend's arm round the shoulders as friendship in that culture, and still being free to refuse touch he dislikes.

passage: Tanvir came off the debate stage at the district competition knowing they'd lost. He sat on the bench in the corridor, jaw tight, staring at his shoes. His coach, Vandana Ma'am, sat down at the other end. “Tough round,” she said. “Can I pat your back?” Tanvir shrugged, then nodded. Her hand gave two light pats between his shoulders and was gone. Tanvir felt something in his chest loosen. It wasn't pity, he decided. It was the same pat she gave the winners, just quieter. “Your rebuttal was your best yet,” she said. He looked up. “Really?” “Really. Next year.”

qa.q: Where did Tanvir sit after the debate?
qa.a: Tanvir sat on the bench in the corridor.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling as he stared at his shoes?
qa.a: Tanvir felt disappointed and tense after losing, his jaw tight.

qa.q: Why did Vandana Ma'am ask before patting him?
qa.a: Asking let Tanvir choose, which respected him and made the pat feel like reassurance rather than something done to him.

qa.q: What was Vandana Ma'am trying to show with the pat and her words?
qa.a: She wanted to reassure him and show she valued his effort, especially his rebuttal, even though they lost.

grounding: Shows a child reading a teacher's pat on the back as reassurance, offered with a question so it could be refused.

passage: I'm Seema, and I walk to the bus stop with Gautam most days. In our colony, boys often walk holding hands or with arms round each other; it's just friendship. But this week an older boy from the next building kept grabbing Gautam's hand and squeezing it hard, not letting go when Gautam tugged. Gautam's face went tight, and he kept looking at me. Yesterday Gautam pulled free and said loudly, “Don't. I don't like it.” The older boy laughed and walked off. I don't know everything Gautam felt. But at the stop he told his mother, who was waiting there, and she went to the older boy's parents that same evening.

qa.q: Where do Seema and Gautam walk most days?
qa.a: They walk to the bus stop.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling when his face went tight?
qa.a: Gautam felt uncomfortable and uneasy with the hard, unwanted squeezing, unlike friendly hand-holding.

qa.q: What did Gautam do that was right?
qa.a: He clearly said no to the touch and told his mother, a trusted adult, the same day.

qa.q: How does Seema tell this touch apart from friendly hand-holding?
qa.a: Seema notices Gautam tugging away, his tight face and the older boy not letting go, which friendly hand-holding doesn't involve.

grounding: Shows friendly hand-holding among boys as normal friendship, and a child refusing and reporting touch that made him uncomfortable.

passage:
Monday: Jasleen and Navpreet walked to school hand in hand, swinging their arms like always. Her cousin Hrithik, visiting from Toronto, smirked. "Are you two a couple?" Jasleen rolled her eyes. "She's my best friend. Here lots of friends do this."

Wednesday: After Jasleen's shaky dance at assembly, Mrs Gill patted her twice on the back. "Brave effort." Jasleen's shoulders relaxed. A pat from Ma'am meant well done.

Friday: At tuition, a boy grabbed her wrist to drag her into tag and wouldn't let go. It didn't feel like a friend's hand. "Let go. I don't like that," she said, and pulled free. She told the tuition teacher straight away. The teacher spoke to the boy right then and told Jasleen she was right to say no and to tell.

qa.q: Where was Hrithik visiting from?
qa.a: From Toronto.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling on Friday when the boy wouldn't let go of her wrist?
qa.a: Uncomfortable and uneasy, because it didn't feel like a friend's hand; she was firm enough to say no and pull free.

qa.q: What did Jasleen do on Friday that was wise?
qa.a: She said clearly, "Let go. I don't like that," pulled free and told the tuition teacher straight away.

qa.q: How did Hrithik read the hand-holding on Monday?
qa.a: Hrithik read it as romance, perhaps because friends there hold hands less often; for Jasleen it simply meant friendship.

grounding: It shows a child reading hand-holding and a teacher's pat as friendship and reassurance, and refusing and reporting a touch that felt wrong.
